name: Bryan Johnson Blueprint diet
lead: The Blueprint diet is the largely vegan eating plan that American entrepreneur Bryan Johnson follows as part of Blueprint, his longevity protocol announced in October 2021 as Project Blueprint and later a company sold under the slogan "Don't Die".[1] Johnson says his goal is to lower the biological age of his organs, with Fortune reporting a stated aim of organs matching those of an 18-year-old, and he publishes his meals, supplements and biomarker results.[1]

In appearance communities the diet is followed as a template for looking younger for longer: a plant-heavy, early-finishing meal pattern, measured against tracked biomarkers, is meant to support skin, body composition and healthy-looking ageing. Wikipedia reports that Johnson eats an entirely plant-based diet except for collagen peptides, and that he says this is separate from the Blueprint protocol itself.[1]

Grokipedia describes a plan of three meals ending by 11 a.m., with items such as a vegetable-and-lentil meal, olive oil and a nut-based pudding.[2] No clinical trial has tested the diet, results are self-reported from one individual, and experts quoted in coverage say biomarker changes do not establish slowed aging.[1][2]

paras: Wikipedia reports that Johnson eats an entirely plant-based diet except for collagen peptides [1]. Grokipedia, which is AI-generated, describes meals such as broccoli, cauliflower and black lentils with olive oil, and a final meal of sweet potato, chickpeas and avocado, with no food after 11 a.m. It also gives calorie figures that are inconsistent within the page [2].

Johnson, who sold Braintree to PayPal in 2013, moved from standard health measures toward anti-aging experiments in 2021 and announced Project Blueprint on 13 October 2021. It later became a Los Angeles company that sells supplements and foods modelled on his protocol [1]. A Netflix documentary, Don't Die, appeared in 2025 [1].

Wikipedia reports that Johnson tracks over 100 health measurements, that the protocol cost about $2 million a year in 2023, and that Blueprint Basics launched in 2024 at $333 per month.[1] By March 2026 he had reduced his daily supplements from 111 to 30.[1]
No studies found. Johnson's reported results, such as a DunedinPACE score of about 0.5 years of biological aging per calendar year in 2025, are self-measured from one person [1][2].

Moshe Szyf of McGill University has doubted that science can yet produce the claimed results, and longevity researcher Andrew Steele has said no regimen changes a person's genes [1]. Gerontology researchers quoted by Grokipedia say epigenetic clocks do not prove slowed aging [2]. Wikipedia also reports a 2025 New York Times investigation into his use of confidentiality agreements, and his June 2026 announcement of an autoimmune gastritis diagnosis, which he said was not caused by his regimen [1].

In 2023 Johnson received monthly plasma transfusions over six months, including one from his 17-year-old son; he has said he will not repeat them because they showed no benefit, and the FDA has said such transfusions have no demonstrated benefit and may be harmful.[1]

lore.intro: Followers treat Johnson's published meals as a template for aging well and skin quality; his results are widely shared.

claims.claim: The Blueprint diet reverses biological aging.
claims.believers: Johnson reports slowed pace-of-aging scores and younger organ ages [1].
claims.experts: Researchers say epigenetic clocks do not prove slowed aging and no trial tests the protocol [2].

claims.claim: Eating early and finishing by late morning supports longevity.
claims.believers: Johnson describes a compressed eating window [2].
claims.experts: No published studies have examined this specific schedule in his protocol.

card.summary: The mostly vegan, early-eating plan of longevity entrepreneur Bryan Johnson; widely shared, tested only on himself.
card.note: Single-person self-reported results; no controlled trials.

quick.overview:
The Blueprint diet is the meal plan Bryan Johnson uses as part of his Blueprint longevity protocol. It is mostly plant-based and eaten early in the day, and he publishes his meals and biomarker results.

It is discussed in appearance communities for skin and aging claims. The results come from one person, and experts say they do not establish slowed aging.
quick.mechanism: Johnson says the aim is to lower the biological age of his organs through diet, exercise, sleep and supplements; the diet itself has not been tested separately.
quick.risks: Wikipedia and other coverage report expert skepticism and some controversy around Blueprint products. No trial data on the diet exist.

chain: Eat a measured, plant-based diet in an early window
Slower measured pace of ageing, as Johnson reports
Younger-looking skin and body, as followers hope
angle.text: Followers copy Johnson's published meals and schedule hoping to look and measure younger; the face and body outcomes are his own self-reported results.
